players.product: retail colocation & interconnection (IBX data centers, Equinix Fabric) and xScale hyperscale data centers

quarterly_data.signal: New AI products Fabric One and Inference Exchange. The moderator named both products and said Inference Exchange is a partnership with NVIDIA. President of the Americas Arkell Shaw said 'I think of it as Fabric as the connection and the Exchange as what's operating'. On NVIDIA he said the relationship began with helping customers reach 'the infrastructure that customers needed' and has shifted toward getting inference to the customer: 'Introducing this product was an important part of that journey in terms of working with NVIDIA and also Together AI'. Shaw confirmed ('Yeah') the moderator's suggestion that pricing will be 'more outcome-based', describing it as 'one price based on the outcome that the customer is looking for'.

Deal size and density are stepping up. Shaw: 'Whereas a 250 kVA deal was a large deal for us, a megawatt is kind of the going thing now.' He gave the announced DA12 build as an example: 'we are going to be delivering, I think about 67 megawatts, and it is going to have a density of about 18 kVA per cabinet. That is denser than we have ever gone'. He added that Equinix does 'not build gigawatt data centers to perform training'. Instead, xScale is meant to bring the clouds closer to the dense metro ecosystems. The moderator named the Hertfordshire campus and the Osaka site, and Shaw said 'those are the two right now that we are looking at. They are on track.'
quarterly_data.figure: 250 kVA deal was a large deal; a megawatt is kind of the going thing now; DA12 about 67 megawatts at about 18 kVA per cabinet

quarterly_data.signal: Liquid-cooling strategy is to build it into new sites, not to retrofit old ones. Shaw: 'When we think about new builds, we think about liquid cooling. We're less prone to retrofitting a building for liquid cooling' and 'We're not going back and retrofitting a bunch of buildings for liquid cooling.' He said enterprise demand has changed: liquid-cooled space used to sit empty because customers found it 'really expensive', but 'Now it's a requirement'. The optional design means Equinix is 'not stuck with liquid cooling that we're not utilizing'. CFO Ryan Burke compared the in-cage deployment to 'a NASCAR pit crew': customers who want liquid cooling pay for it, and Equinix can pull it out and deploy it elsewhere when they no longer need it.

Growth math behind the raised long-term outlook. Burke: 'What was our old high end is now our new low end', citing demand that 'came on faster than the company anticipated'. He said 'you can see our same-store pool sort of migrating from mid-single into high digit revenue growth. Then you can expect that capacity expansion will do the rest.' He said it 'takes 2-3 years to lease our properties up to Equinix level of stabilization', which is the mid-20% cash yield. Shaw gave scale and concentration figures: 'almost 11,000 customers', 'over 522,000 interconnections globally', data centers at 'Is it 282 at this point?', and 'no single customer that houses it over about 2.5% of the portfolio'. The moderator, not management, quoted the 9%-12% AFFO per share guidance.

(data centers, speaker unsure); no single customer that houses it over about 2.5% of the portfolio

quarterly_data.signal: Community opposition has not delayed Equinix builds so far. Shaw called backlash 'a real thing' but said Equinix engages community leaders before it buys land. He said 'We just did an extensive one in Minooka that was really well-received' (a town hall about the project) and 'we have not seen some of the delays or issues that have come up.' He also said Equinix has 'always paid for our usage' and invests with power companies to build out the grid it needs.
